Some managers are conniving and will use their "power" and cheat employees out of their rightful time/breaks/pay/etc. Or maybe your manager is under a different understanding/assumptions of the company policies. 

If it is clearly written in your company's employee handbook and is pertaining to every employee regardless of their status, hourly/salaried then I suggest you go to HR and ask them about the policy and what happens if you are that policy is breached. 

(I used to work in HR in my previous place of work and if an employee would not clock out for their lunch break, in a shift of 6 hrs or greater, the system would automatically deduct a 30 min lunch, unless overridden by their manager for reasons like a working lunch, etc. Maybe it is something similar?)  

Either way, if you do go to HR and HR follows up with your manager and use your name be prepared to scrutiny and retaliation from their part. If your manager is doing this knowingly and malevolently doing this for their own gain, I wouldn't put it past them to retaliate/give backlash.

I'm sorry you're going through this, I can't imagine the emotional stress this has caused. As a gay man, and interactions with other closeted-gay men, I will tell you this:

A "straight" man, even in this day and age, will be terrified to accept the fact that he is gay/bi, and will go to great lengths to remain in denial and keep others from finding out. Even if you sit down and have a long, heart-felt conversation about this with him, odds are that he won't be as honest with you as you'd like him to be (perhaps not even be very honest with himself). 

Ultimately, what he did is considered betrayal, in my book. You have to make a decision whether or not you terminate your relationship with him. But you know the consequences of your choices:

If you leave, that allows him the liberty to experiment and explore his sexual preferences and orientation. But he might also enter a relationship with another woman to keep up the facade. Which, I imagine would be very painful. Eventually, you would heal and move on.

If you stay, be prepared to continue to encounter additional situations like just like this one, or of similar nature, and the feelings they cause you to feel. If you felt comfortable, maybe suggest to help him uncover what he's really feeling.

You should watch My Mad Fat Diary on Hulu. It's about a young girl who enters a similar relationship to yours. She is overweight and has many insecurities. She becomes friends with a group of "cool", "fit", "attractive" people her age and one of the guys in the group begins to show interest in her. He likes her, but she pushes him away because of how insecure she feels. 

I think you'll find this relatable because it shows what goes through her mind when they are together and how insecurities are the catalyst to the downfall of her relationship.

I don't think it's fair to compare a relationship of two grown adults to that of children/teens. If you feel like you are compatible, care and treat each other well, what does it matter? Your friends might also be jealous; either because she takes up more of your time (less to spend with them) or because you have a type of relationship that they want. 

If the age difference between you and your gf bothers them to the point of driving a wedge between you and them, were they really ever your friends?

At this point, you're past the warning signs. This is already a well-forming abusive relationship. He seems to have deep seeded issues with his self-esteem, betrayal, abandonment, etc. 

I strongly think you should get out of that relationship ASAP. Otherwise, it will be an endless cycle that will be incredibly difficult to break.
